title: Theatre & Dialogue
subtitle: Read the theatrical text like a dramaturge, write dialogue that breathes, and think through a director's staging choices

lessons.title: Le texte théâtral
lessons.description: Learn to read a play script as its own genre: how didascalies direct the actor, how register signals class and relationship, and the conventions — aparté, tirade, quiproquo — unique to dramatic dialogue.

blocks.heading: Les didascalies : la voix de l'auteur dans la marge
blocks.body: A play script has two distinct voices: the dialogue, spoken by characters, and the didascalies — the playwright's stage directions, printed in italics or parentheses. Didascalies rarely use full sentences with a conjugated subject; they favour nominal sentences (Un temps.), present-tense verbs (Elle sort.), or present participles (Se retournant brusquement.) because they describe action happening now, for a reader who must picture it instantly. Reading a play well means never skipping them: they carry tone, tempo, and staging information dialogue alone cannot.

examples.french: (Un temps. Elle regarde la porte, puis renonce.)
examples.english: (A pause. She looks at the door, then gives up.)

examples.french: (Bas, sans se retourner.) Tu savais.
examples.english: (Quietly, without turning round.) You knew.

examples.french: MARGUERITE, s'approchant. — Tu ne réponds jamais directement.
examples.english: MARGUERITE, approaching. — You never answer directly.

examples.french: (Silence. On entend la pluie contre la vitre.)
examples.english: (Silence. Rain can be heard against the window.)

examples.french: (Elle hésite, puis referme la lettre sans la lire.)
examples.english: (She hesitates, then closes the letter again without reading it.)

blocks.tip: A didascalie in the present participle (Se retournant..., Hésitant...) almost always describes an action simultaneous with the line that follows — stage it, don't narrate it.

blocks.heading: Le registre : faire entendre une classe, une époque, une relation
blocks.body: Because a play has no narrator to explain who a character is, register does that work instead. A line in registre soutenu signals education, formality, or emotional distance; the same idea in registre familier signals intimacy, youth, or social ease. A skilled dramaturge shifts a single character's register mid-scene to mark a change in power or feeling — dropping into the familiar the moment a mask slips.

examples.french: Il conviendrait, Madame, que vous m'expliquiez enfin la vérité.
examples.english: It would be fitting, Madam, for you to finally explain the truth to me.

examples.french: Bon, tu me le dis ou pas, ce qui s'est passé ?
examples.english: Right, are you going to tell me what happened or not?

examples.french: Je vous prie de croire, Monsieur, à toute ma considération — et à tout mon mépris.
examples.english: Please believe, Sir, in all my regard — and all my contempt.

examples.french: T'as pas le droit de me parler comme ça, pas ici, pas devant eux.
examples.english: You've got no right to talk to me like that, not here, not in front of them.

examples.french: Le registre bascule dès que le masque tombe : la politesse cède au tutoiement rageur.
examples.english: The register flips the moment the mask falls: politeness gives way to furious informality.

blocks.tip: Watch for a sudden switch from vous to tu within one scene — in a script it almost always marks a dramatic turning point, not carelessness.

blocks.heading: Les conventions du dialogue dramatique
blocks.body: Theatre has its own toolkit for saying things a novel would simply narrate. L'aparté lets a character speak a private thought the others on stage cannot hear. La tirade is one character's uninterrupted long speech, held together by rhythm as much as by argument. Le quiproquo — a misunderstanding built on crossed information — drives both comedy and tragedy, since the audience knows the truth the characters don't.

examples.french: (Aparté.) S'il savait ce que je sais, il ne sourirait pas ainsi.
examples.english: (Aside.) If he knew what I know, he wouldn't be smiling like that.

examples.french: Sa tirade final dure près de trois minutes sans qu'aucun autre personnage n'intervienne.
examples.english: His final tirade lasts nearly three minutes without any other character speaking.

examples.french: Le quiproquo naît d'une simple lettre mal adressée, et personne ne le découvre avant l'acte trois.
examples.english: The mix-up arises from a simple misaddressed letter, and no one discovers it before act three.

examples.french: Le public rit précisément parce qu'il connaît la vérité que les personnages ignorent.
examples.english: The audience laughs precisely because it knows the truth the characters do not.

examples.french: Une bonne tirade se construit comme une phrase de musicien : elle respire avant de conclure.
examples.english: A good tirade is built like a musician's phrase: it breathes before it concludes.

blocks.tip: In print, an aparté is often marked simply '(Aparté.)' or '(À part.)' before the line — both mean the same convention.

items.example: Les didascalies précisent que la scène se passe à l'aube.
items.exampleEnglish: The stage directions specify that the scene takes place at dawn.

items.example: Le dramaturge refuse toute didascalie psychologique, préférant l'action nue.
items.exampleEnglish: The playwright refuses any psychological stage direction, preferring bare action.

items.example: Cette pièce de théâtre repose presque entièrement sur un unique quiproquo.
items.exampleEnglish: This play rests almost entirely on a single misunderstanding.

items.example: Le quiproquo n'est révélé qu'au troisième acte.
items.exampleEnglish: The mix-up is revealed only in the third act.

items.example: La scène s'ouvre sur un silence que personne n'ose rompre.
items.exampleEnglish: The scene opens on a silence no one dares to break.

items.example: Sa dernière réplique tombe comme un couperet, sans un mot de trop.
items.exampleEnglish: His last line falls like a blade, without a word too many.

items.example: Le dialogue avance par sous-entendus plus que par affirmations.
items.exampleEnglish: The dialogue advances through insinuation more than through statement.

items.example: Chaque personnage entre en scène avec son propre registre.
items.exampleEnglish: Each character enters with their own register.

items.example: Le protagoniste ne prononce pas un mot avant la troisième scène.
items.exampleEnglish: The protagonist does not utter a word before the third scene.

items.example: L'antagoniste n'apparaît jamais sur scène, seulement dans les répliques des autres.
items.exampleEnglish: The antagonist never appears on stage, only in the other characters' lines.

items.example: C'est un rôle écrit presque entièrement en registre soutenu.
items.exampleEnglish: It's a role written almost entirely in a formal register.

items.example: Le comédien doit tenir la tirade sans jamais perdre le fil.
items.exampleEnglish: The actor has to sustain the tirade without ever losing the thread.

items.example: L'aparté révèle au public ce qu'aucun personnage sur scène ne sait encore.
items.exampleEnglish: The aside reveals to the audience what no character on stage yet knows.

items.example: Le monologue final se joue seule, face public, dans une lumière crue.
items.exampleEnglish: The final monologue is played alone, facing the audience, in a harsh light.

items.english: the tirade, the long uninterrupted speech
items.example: L'acteur enchaîne la tirade sans reprendre son souffle.
items.exampleEnglish: The actor delivers the tirade without pausing for breath.

items.example: Tout repose sur un quiproquo que le spectateur perce avant les personnages.
items.exampleEnglish: Everything rests on a mix-up the spectator sees through before the characters do.

items.example: Le registre change dès que les deux frères se retrouvent seuls.
items.exampleEnglish: The register changes as soon as the two brothers are alone together.

items.example: Ce personnage ne s'exprime qu'en registre soutenu, même sous la menace.
items.exampleEnglish: This character speaks only in a formal register, even under threat.

items.example: Le passage au registre familier trahit sa panique.
items.exampleEnglish: The shift to a colloquial register betrays his panic.

items.example: La plupart des répliques restent en registre courant, sans effet appuyé.
items.exampleEnglish: Most of the lines stay in a standard register, without a heavy effect.

items.example: La pièce se présente comme une comédie, mais glisse peu à peu vers le drame.
items.exampleEnglish: The play presents itself as a comedy, but gradually slides towards drama.

items.example: La tragédie exige que le dénouement soit connu d'avance.
items.exampleEnglish: Tragedy demands that the ending be known in advance.

items.example: Ce drame refuse aussi bien le pathos que l'ironie.
items.exampleEnglish: This drama refuses both pathos and irony.

items.example: L'effet comique tient tout entier au décalage entre les deux répliques.
items.exampleEnglish: The comic effect rests entirely on the gap between the two lines.

items.example: Le ton reste tragique jusque dans les répliques les plus brèves.
items.exampleEnglish: The tone stays tragic even in the briefest lines.

items.example: Le texte ne précise jamais l'âge du personnage principal.
items.exampleEnglish: The text never specifies the main character's age.

items.example: L'auteur laisse volontairement le dénouement ouvert.
items.exampleEnglish: The author deliberately leaves the ending open.

items.example: Parler seul à voix haute n'est acceptable que par convention théâtrale.
items.exampleEnglish: Speaking alone out loud is acceptable only by theatrical convention.

items.example: Le personnage brise soudain le quatrième mur pour interroger la salle.
items.exampleEnglish: The character suddenly breaks the fourth wall to question the audience.

items.english: the direct address to the audience
items.example: L'adresse au public, rare dans cette pièce, marque un tournant.
items.exampleEnglish: The direct address to the audience, rare in this play, marks a turning point.

items.example: L'intrigue tient tout entière dans une lettre jamais ouverte.
items.exampleEnglish: The whole plot rests on a letter that is never opened.

items.example: Le dénouement se joue en trois répliques à peine.
items.exampleEnglish: The resolution plays out in barely three lines.

items.english: the dramatic crux, the knot of the plot
items.example: Le nœud dramatique se noue autour d'un simple malentendu de nom.
items.exampleEnglish: The dramatic crux ties itself around a simple mix-up of names.

items.example: Le conflit oppose deux registres autant que deux volontés.
items.exampleEnglish: The conflict pits two registers against each other as much as two wills.

items.english: what is at stake, the key issue
items.example: L'enjeu de la scène n'apparaît clairement qu'à la dernière réplique.
items.exampleEnglish: What is at stake in the scene only becomes clear on the last line.

items.example: Le quiproquo reste vraisemblable parce qu'il repose sur un simple hasard.
items.exampleEnglish: The mix-up stays believable because it rests on simple chance.

items.example: Le ton bascule du comique au tragique en une seule réplique.
items.exampleEnglish: The tone swings from comic to tragic within a single line.

items.example: On reconnaît chaque personnage à sa seule voix, sans nom en tête de réplique.
items.exampleEnglish: Each character is recognisable by voice alone, without a name heading the line.

blocks.heading: Le mode des didascalies : phrases nominales et participes présents
blocks.body: Didascalies rarely take a full conjugated clause with a subject and finite verb. Instead they favour the nominal sentence (a noun phrase with no verb at all: Un temps. Silence.), the bare present tense for an action described as it happens (Elle sort.), or a present participle clause describing something simultaneous with the line it precedes (Se retournant, elle...). This compression is deliberate: a didascalie is read in an instant, so it must be grammatically as compact as the moment it stages.

examples.french: Un temps. Elle repose la tasse sans bruit.
examples.english: A pause. She sets the cup down without a sound.

examples.french: (Riant, malgré elle.) Tu es impossible.
examples.english: (Laughing, in spite of herself.) You're impossible.

examples.french: Silence. Puis, très bas : c'était donc toi.
examples.english: Silence. Then, very quietly: so it was you.

examples.french: (S'avançant vers la fenêtre.) Il ne reviendra pas ce soir.
examples.english: (Moving towards the window.) He won't be back tonight.

examples.french: (Hésitant, puis se décidant.) Je vais tout te dire.
examples.english: (Hesitating, then making up her mind.) I'm going to tell you everything.

blocks.tip: A nominal didascalie like 'Un temps.' or 'Silence.' has no verb at all — resist the urge to translate it as a full English sentence; keep the English just as bare.

blocks.heading: Le discours direct sans verbe introducteur
blocks.body: A novel tags speech with dit-il, répondit-elle. A play never does: the character's name printed before the line does that job instead, so the dialogue itself stays pure direct discourse, unfiltered by any narrator. This has a grammatical consequence — a playwright can let a reply begin mid-thought, without the connecting tissue (elle ajouta que, il reprit) a narrated dialogue would need to link one turn to the next.

examples.french: CLAIRE. — Tu mens. MARC. — Depuis toujours.
examples.english: CLAIRE. — You're lying. MARC. — I always have.

examples.french: Aucun 'dit-il' ne sépare ces deux répliques : le nom en tête de ligne suffit.
examples.english: No 'he said' separates these two lines: the name at the head of the line is enough.

examples.french: LE PÈRE. — Et si je refusais ? LA FILLE. — Tu ne refuseras pas.
examples.english: THE FATHER. — And if I refused? THE DAUGHTER. — You won't refuse.

examples.french: La réplique suivante commence sans transition, comme si elle coupait la parole à la précédente.
examples.english: The next line begins with no transition, as if it were cutting off the previous one.

examples.french: En passant du roman à la pièce, on supprime tous les verbes de parole.
examples.english: In moving from the novel to the play, every speech verb is removed.

blocks.tip: When you adapt narrated dialogue into a script, delete every dit-il/répondit-elle — the character name heading the line already carries that function.

passages.title: Les Heures grises — Acte II, scène 3 (Élise Fontaine)
passages.french:
(Le salon d'une vieille maison. Il pleut. MARGUERITE range des lettres sur la table basse.)
LOUIS, entrant sans frapper. — Tu n'as pas répondu à mon message.
MARGUERITE, sans lever les yeux. — Quel message ?
LOUIS. — Ne joue pas à ça avec moi.
(Un temps. Elle repose la lettre qu'elle tenait.)
MARGUERITE. — Il conviendrait, Louis, que tu m'expliques d'abord pourquoi tu es venu.
LOUIS. — Bon, tu veux vraiment qu'on fasse ça en registre soutenu ?
MARGUERITE, souriant malgré elle. — Ça te va si mal, la politesse.
(Silence. On entend la pluie contre la vitre.)
LOUIS, plus bas. — J'ai trouvé la lettre. Celle que tu croyais brûlée.
MARGUERITE, aparté. — S'il savait à qui elle était adressée, il ne serait pas si calme.
LOUIS. — Tu ne dis rien ?
MARGUERITE. — Qu'est-ce que tu veux que je dise ?
LOUIS. — La vérité, pour une fois.
(Elle hésite, puis referme la boîte à lettres sans un mot.)
MARGUERITE. — La vérité, Louis, c'est que tu as ouvert une lettre qui n'était pas pour toi.
passages.english:
(The living room of an old house. It is raining. MARGUERITE tidies letters on the coffee table.)
LOUIS, entering without knocking. — You didn't answer my message.
MARGUERITE, without looking up. — What message?
LOUIS. — Don't play that game with me.
(A pause. She sets down the letter she was holding.)
MARGUERITE. — It would be fitting, Louis, for you to first explain why you've come.
LOUIS. — Right, do you really want to do this in a formal register?
MARGUERITE, smiling in spite of herself. — Politeness suits you so badly.
(Silence. Rain can be heard against the window.)
LOUIS, more quietly. — I found the letter. The one you thought was burnt.
MARGUERITE, aside. — If he knew who it was addressed to, he wouldn't be so calm.
LOUIS. — You're not saying anything?
MARGUERITE. — What do you want me to say?
LOUIS. — The truth, for once.
(She hesitates, then closes the letter box again without a word.)
MARGUERITE. — The truth, Louis, is that you opened a letter that wasn't for you.

lessons.title: Écrire un dialogue vivant
lessons.description: Move from correct dialogue to dialogue that feels alive: control rhythm through line length and pause, plant subtext beneath what characters actually say, and use interruption and hesitation to sound unscripted.

blocks.heading: Le rythme : la longueur de la réplique comme instrument
blocks.body: Rhythm in dialogue is largely a matter of line length. A run of short répliques — one or two words each — reads fast and tense, like a exchange neither character controls. A single long tirade slows everything down and hands one character the floor. Skilled dialogue alternates deliberately: build tension with clipped exchanges, then release it by letting one voice finally speak at length.

examples.french: — Pars. — Non. — Pars, je te dis. — Non.
examples.english: "Go." "No." "Go, I'm telling you." "No."

examples.french: Quatre répliques d'un mot suffisent à faire monter la tension bien mieux qu'une explication.
examples.english: Four one-word lines raise the tension far better than an explanation would.

examples.french: Après ce silence, elle se lance enfin dans une longue tirade que personne n'interrompt.
examples.english: After that silence, she finally launches into a long speech that no one interrupts.

examples.french: Le débit s'accélère à mesure que la dispute se resserre.
examples.english: The pace of delivery speeds up as the argument tightens.

examples.french: Casser le rythme d'un coup, par une réplique très courte, frappe plus fort qu'un cri.
examples.english: Suddenly breaking the rhythm with a very short line hits harder than a shout.

blocks.tip: Count the syllables of consecutive lines when a scene feels flat on the page — real tension usually shows up as a visible shrinking pattern, long line, shorter, shorter, one word.

blocks.heading: Le sous-texte : dire une chose, en vouloir une autre
blocks.body: In life, people rarely say exactly what they mean; good dialogue respects that. Le sous-texte is the real feeling or intention running beneath the literal words of a line — l'implicite the audience must infer, and le sous-entendu a character deliberately plants for another to catch. A line about the weather can carry an entire unspoken accusation, as long as the actor and the audience both know it.

examples.french: « Tu as l'air fatigué » ne parle jamais vraiment de fatigue dans cette scène.
examples.english: "You look tired" is never really about tiredness in this scene.

examples.french: Le sous-texte de cette réplique, c'est une accusation qu'aucun des deux ne formule.
examples.english: The subtext of this line is an accusation neither of them puts into words.

examples.french: Elle ne dit jamais qu'elle est jalouse ; tout l'implicite tient dans ce silence.
examples.english: She never says she's jealous; the whole implication lies in that silence.

examples.french: Le sous-entendu passe inaperçu du personnage visé, mais pas du spectateur.
examples.english: The insinuation goes unnoticed by the character it targets, but not by the spectator.

examples.french: Écrire du sous-texte, c'est faire confiance à l'acteur pour porter ce que le mot ne dit pas.
examples.english: Writing subtext means trusting the actor to carry what the word does not say.

blocks.tip: If a line says exactly what a character feels, ask what they would actually say instead — real subtext usually hides behind a deflection, a question, or small talk.

blocks.heading: L'interruption, l'hésitation, le naturel de l'échange
blocks.body: Nobody finishes every sentence in real conversation. Written dialogue that lets characters interrompre one another, hésiter mid-thought, or couper la parole to a partner reads as far more spontané and naturel than dialogue where every line is grammatically complete. Overuse this and the scene turns to chaos, but a well-placed interruption is often the single most convincing detail in a scene.

examples.french: — Je voulais juste te dire que— — Je sais déjà.
examples.english: "I just wanted to tell you that—" "I already know."

examples.french: Il l'interrompt avant qu'elle finisse sa phrase, et elle le laisse faire.
examples.english: He interrupts her before she finishes her sentence, and she lets him.

examples.french: Elle hésite sur chaque mot, comme si la phrase se construisait devant nous.
examples.english: She hesitates over every word, as if the sentence were being built in front of us.

examples.french: Couper la parole à quelqu'un, sur scène, dit souvent plus qu'une longue réplique.
examples.english: Cutting someone off, on stage, often says more than a long line.

examples.french: Cette joute verbale ne laisse à aucun des deux le temps de respirer.
examples.english: This verbal sparring match leaves neither of them time to breathe.

blocks.tip: Mark an interruption with an em dash at the exact syllable where the second character cuts in — not at the end of the first character's grammatical sentence.

blocks.heading: Phrases nominales et ellipse syntaxique
blocks.body: Realistic dialogue drops words a full written sentence would keep. A phrase nominale states a noun with no verb at all (Encore toi.); syntactic ellipsis lets a character skip a subject, a verb, or an entire clause the listener can reconstruct from context. Both devices compress a line toward how people actually speak — in fragments, trusting the other person to fill the gap.

examples.french: Encore toi. Toujours au mauvais moment.
examples.english: You again. Always at the worst moment.

examples.french: — Tu pars quand ? — Demain, peut-être.
examples.english: "When are you leaving?" "Tomorrow, maybe."

examples.french: Rien à faire. Rien à dire non plus.
examples.english: Nothing to be done. Nothing to say either.

examples.french: — Et si elle refuse ? — Alors on verra.
examples.english: "And if she refuses?" "Then we'll see."

examples.french: Pas un mot de plus. Pas ce soir.
examples.english: Not one more word. Not tonight.

blocks.tip: An ellipsis works only if the missing words are recoverable from the previous line — cut too much and the exchange stops making sense rather than sounding natural.

blocks.heading: La ponctuation de l'interruption : tiret et points de suspension
blocks.body: French playtexts mark spoken interruption with two distinct tools. The tiret cadratif (em dash) at the end of a line shows a character cut off mid-word or mid-thought by another; les points de suspension (…) show a character trailing off on their own, unable or unwilling to finish. Choosing between them is a choice about cause: was the silence imposed from outside, or chosen from within?

examples.french: MARC. — Je voulais juste te dire que— CLAIRE. — Je sais déjà.
examples.english: MARC. — I just wanted to tell you that— CLAIRE. — I already know.

examples.french: Elle commence une phrase, puis... rien.
examples.english: She begins a sentence, then... nothing.

examples.french: — Si tu partais maintenant, je— — Ne dis rien.
examples.english: "If you left now, I—" "Don't say anything."

examples.french: Il hésite, cherche ses mots, et finit par se taire.
examples.english: He hesitates, searches for his words, and ends up falling silent.

examples.french: Le tiret coupe la réplique net ; les points de suspension la laissent flotter.
examples.english: The dash cuts the line off sharply; the ellipsis points let it drift.

blocks.tip: Reserve the em dash for a genuine interruption by another character — using it for a character's own trailing thought blurs a distinction actors rely on.

passages.title: Le Bruit des verres — scène (Thomas Nadeau)
passages.french:
(Une cuisine, tard le soir. SOPHIE essuie un verre. DANIEL entre, encore en manteau.)
DANIEL. — Tu ne m'as pas attendu pour manger.
SOPHIE. — J'avais faim.
DANIEL. — Bien sûr.
(Un temps.)
SOPHIE. — Tu voulais dire autre chose ?
DANIEL. — Non.
SOPHIE. — Daniel.
DANIEL. — Je pensais juste que—
SOPHIE. — Que quoi ?
DANIEL. — Rien. Laisse tomber.
(Elle repose le verre, très doucement.)
SOPHIE. — Tu rentres tard, tu dis « rien », et tu gardes ton manteau.
DANIEL. — J'ai froid.
SOPHIE. — Non. Tu as peur.
(Silence. Il ne répond pas.)
passages.english:
(A kitchen, late at night. SOPHIE dries a glass. DANIEL enters, still in his coat.)
DANIEL. — You didn't wait for me to eat.
SOPHIE. — I was hungry.
DANIEL. — Of course.
(A pause.)
SOPHIE. — Did you want to say something else?
DANIEL. — No.
SOPHIE. — Daniel.
DANIEL. — I was just thinking that—
SOPHIE. — That what?
DANIEL. — Nothing. Forget it.
(She sets down the glass, very gently.)
SOPHIE. — You come home late, you say "nothing," and you keep your coat on.
DANIEL. — I'm cold.
SOPHIE. — No. You're afraid.
(Silence. He does not answer.)

lessons.title: La mise en scène
lessons.description: Move from the page to the stage: read a text the way a director does, weighing choices about décor, era, and fidelity, then judge whether a staging is convincing.

blocks.heading: La lecture du texte : le point de départ du metteur en scène
blocks.body: Before a single décor is built, le metteur en scène produces une lecture — a personal, arguable interpretation of what the text is really about. Two directors can stage the same text with opposite results because they answered a different question first: is this a play about power, about grief, about language itself? Every later choice, from le décor to le rythme des répliques, follows from that initial reading.

examples.french: Sa lecture de la pièce privilégie le pouvoir plutôt que l'amour.
examples.english: Her reading of the play foregrounds power rather than love.

examples.french: Le metteur en scène part d'une question simple : de quoi ce texte parle-t-il vraiment ?
examples.english: The director starts from a simple question: what is this text really about?

examples.french: Deux lectures opposées peuvent naître d'un seul et même texte.
examples.english: Two opposing readings can arise from one and the same text.

examples.french: Le choix du décor découle directement de cette première lecture.
examples.english: The choice of set follows directly from that first reading.

examples.french: On ne monte jamais un texte de manière neutre : on en propose toujours une interprétation.
examples.english: One never stages a text neutrally: one always proposes an interpretation of it.

blocks.tip: When you evaluate a production, ask first what question the director seems to be answering — most staging choices make sense only once you've named it.

blocks.heading: Fidélité et trahison : jusqu'où adapter ?
blocks.body: Every mise en scène balances fidélité to the text against the freedom to make it speak to a present audience. Rester fidèle can mean respecting the period, the punctuation, even the didascalies; trahir le texte — a phrase directors use almost affectionately — means altering it in ways the author never specified. Setting a classical text in a contemporain world is not automatically a betrayal, provided the choice serves the text's own logic rather than replacing it.

examples.french: Cette mise en scène reste fidèle à la lettre, mais réinvente l'esprit du texte.
examples.english: This production stays faithful to the letter, but reinvents the spirit of the text.

examples.french: On l'accuse de trahir le texte en supprimant la moitié des didascalies.
examples.english: He is accused of betraying the text by cutting half the stage directions.

examples.french: Transposer la pièce dans un monde contemporain n'est pas, en soi, une trahison.
examples.english: Moving the play into a contemporary world is not, in itself, a betrayal.

examples.french: La fidélité au texte ne garantit pas, à elle seule, une mise en scène réussie.
examples.english: Faithfulness to the text does not, on its own, guarantee a successful production.

examples.french: Toute adaptation suppose des choix que le texte original ne dictait pas.
examples.english: Every adaptation involves choices the original text did not dictate.

blocks.tip: In director interviews, 'trahir le texte' is rarely a confession of failure — it usually introduces the director's proudest, most deliberate choice.

blocks.heading: Diriger les comédiens, juger le résultat
blocks.body: On stage, the director's reading becomes real through le comédien: diriger an actor means shaping how they incarnent a role without simply dictating line readings. Judging a production afterwards calls for the same vocabulary critics use elsewhere — is the choice convaincant, is the performance crédible, does the whole stay vraisemblable — but applied now to a director's vraisemblance, not just a writer's.

examples.french: Diriger un comédien, ce n'est pas lui imposer une intonation, mais l'aider à la trouver.
examples.english: Directing an actor is not imposing an intonation on them, but helping them find it.

examples.french: Elle incarne ce rôle avec une sobriété qui sert magnifiquement le texte.
examples.english: She embodies this role with a restraint that magnificently serves the text.

examples.french: Le choix d'un décor dépouillé rend l'ensemble d'autant plus convaincant.
examples.english: The choice of a pared-down set makes the whole all the more convincing.

examples.french: La vraisemblance de cette mise en scène tient à un détail : personne ne surjoue.
examples.english: This production's plausibility rests on one detail: no one overacts.

examples.french: Un parti pris audacieux ne vaut que s'il reste crédible du début à la fin.
examples.english: A bold directorial choice is only worth it if it stays credible from beginning to end.

blocks.tip: When praising a director's work, separate two questions — was the parti pris interesting, and was its execution convaincant — a production can succeed at one and fail at the other.

blocks.heading: Formuler une lecture hypothétique : conditionnel et subjonctif
blocks.body: Because a directorial reading is a proposal, not a fact, French criticism reaches for the conditionnel to float it (on pourrait imaginer que..., il faudrait que...) and for the subjonctif once a value judgement or necessity is attached to that proposal. 'Il faudrait que le décor soit nu' does not describe an existing set; it argues for one. Mastering this pair lets you discuss staging choices as possibilities worth defending, not settled facts.

examples.french: On pourrait imaginer une mise en scène entièrement muette.
examples.english: One could imagine a completely wordless production.

examples.french: Il faudrait que le décor soit aussi nu que possible pour que le texte respire.

blocks.tip: 'Il faudrait que' always triggers the subjunctive that follows — treat the two as a fixed pair when you're proposing a staging idea rather than reporting one.

blocks.heading: Nuancer et concéder : bien que, quoique, alors même que
blocks.body: Judging a production well means conceding a point before qualifying it. Bien que and quoique (both followed by the subjunctive) grant that something is true before pivoting to a 'but'; alors même que sharpens the contrast further, insisting the concession makes the criticism more surprising, not less. This is the connective tissue of sophisticated theatre criticism — it keeps praise and reservation in the same sentence instead of two separate paragraphs.

examples.french: Bien que le parti pris soit audacieux, il reste parfaitement lisible.
examples.english: Although the directorial choice is bold, it remains perfectly legible.

examples.french: Quoique la scénographie soit minimaliste, elle ne manque jamais de force.
examples.english: Although the set design is minimalist, it never lacks force.

examples.french: Alors même que le texte est respecté à la lettre, la lecture proposée surprend.
examples.english: Even though the text is respected to the letter, the reading proposed is surprising.

examples.french: La mise en scène convainc, bien qu'elle prenne quelques libertés avec le dénouement.
examples.english: The production convinces, although it takes a few liberties with the ending.

examples.french: Quoi qu'il en soit du parti pris initial, l'exécution force le respect.
examples.english: Whatever one thinks of the initial directorial choice, the execution commands respect.

blocks.tip: Quoique (one word, subjunctive) and quoi que (two words, meaning 'whatever') are not interchangeable — mixing them up is a common but very visible C1 slip.

passages.title: Note d'intention — Camille Aubert, metteuse en scène
passages.french:
Monter « Le Miroir brisé » aujourd'hui pose une question simple : ce texte, écrit pour un monde disparu, a-t-il encore quelque chose à nous dire ?
J'ai choisi de répondre par une lecture résolument contemporaine, sans pour autant changer un seul mot du texte original.
Le décor reste volontairement dépouillé : une chaise, une fenêtre, rien qui distraie du dialogue.
Cette sobriété n'est pas un manque de moyens, c'est un parti pris assumé depuis la première répétition.
On m'a parfois accusée de trahir l'esprit de la pièce en modernisant les costumes.
Je crois au contraire que la fidélité ne se mesure pas aux vêtements, mais au rythme des répliques.
Chaque comédien a travaillé le texte comme une partition, avec ses silences autant que ses mots.
Diriger cette troupe, c'était surtout leur apprendre à ne pas avoir peur du silence.
Le public, au début des répétitions ouvertes, semblait déconcerté par la lenteur du premier acte.
Il a fallu lui faire confiance : la lenteur n'est vraisemblable que si elle est tenue jusqu'au bout.
L'éclairage, très bas, ne s'anime qu'au moment du dénouement, comme un aveu que la scène retenait depuis le début.
Certains critiques jugeront peut-être cette mise en scène trop austère, et ils n'auront pas tort.
Mais je préfère un parti pris cohérent à un compromis qui plairait à tout le monde sans convaincre personne.
Le texte de Julien Mercier survit, je crois, précisément parce qu'il résiste à toute lecture confortable.
Cette mise en scène ne cherche pas à plaire ; elle cherche à rester fidèle à cette résistance-là.
Le rideau tombe sur un silence que j'espère aussi inconfortable pour le public qu'il l'a été pour nous.
passages.english:
Staging "The Broken Mirror" today raises a simple question: does this text, written for a vanished world, still have something to tell us?
I chose to answer with a resolutely contemporary reading, without changing a single word of the original text.
The set remains deliberately bare: a chair, a window, nothing that distracts from the dialogue.
This restraint is not a lack of means; it is a deliberate choice held since the very first rehearsal.
I have sometimes been accused of betraying the spirit of the play by modernising the costumes.
I believe, on the contrary, that faithfulness is not measured in clothing, but in the rhythm of the lines.
Each actor worked the text like a musical score, with its silences as much as its words.
Directing this company was, above all, about teaching them not to fear silence.
The audience, at the early open rehearsals, seemed unsettled by the slowness of the first act.
They had to be trusted: slowness is only believable if it is sustained to the very end.
The lighting, kept very low, only comes alive at the moment of resolution, like a confession the stage had been withholding from the start.
Some critics will perhaps judge this production too austere, and they will not be wrong.
But I prefer a coherent directorial stance to a compromise that would please everyone while convincing no one.
Julien Mercier's text survives, I believe, precisely because it resists any comfortable reading.
This production does not seek to please; it seeks to stay faithful to that very resistance.
The curtain falls on a silence I hope is as uncomfortable for the audience as it was for us.
